solutions.check: grid rebuilt from the blog's light list (unique); every answer written into it with each crossing agreeing

entries.clue: Very large one that makes you feel better (6)

definitions.note: The definition leans on 'one' from the wordplay: read together, 'one that makes you feel better' is the noun.

blocks.note: so = very, as in 'so kind'
L = large, the clothing size
an ace is the one in a pack of cards

annotation.surface: Someone hails a huge thing, perhaps a drink or a meal, as a pick-me-up.
annotation.walkthrough: 'One' does double duty: it is the ACE at the end of the wordplay and also the start of the definition, so the whole clue reads as a description of a comforter.
annotation.definitionFit: A solace is a comfort, something or someone that eases distress.

entries.clue: A little addition reported that’s a surprise (8)

indicators.note: what is reported is heard, so the sound stands in for the spelling

blocks.note: a sum is an addition; said out loud it is SOME
'What!' is an exclamation of surprise

annotation.surface: Someone admits that the news of a small extra came as a shock.
annotation.walkthrough: 'A little' looks like part of 'a little addition' in the surface, but it is the definition standing alone; the homophone covers only SUM, and WHAT is the startled cry.
annotation.definitionFit: Somewhat means to a small degree, just as 'a little' does in 'a little tired'.

entries.clue: Sneaky man checked beneath bait after docking (7)

indicators.note: docking a tail cuts off the end, so LURE loses its last letter
in a down clue, beneath places KING below the bait

blocks.note: LURE (bait) with its last letter cut off
in chess the king is the man that is put in check

annotation.surface: A fisherman slyly checks his line once the boat has docked.
annotation.walkthrough: 'Man' is a chess piece, and the one that gets 'checked' is the king. 'Docking' is the tail-cutting sense, not a boat coming in.
annotation.definitionFit: Lurking describes someone hanging about furtively, out of sight: sneaky.

entries.clue: Attempt to suppress someone who won’t talk quietly, in writing (9)

blocks.note: a clam is a person who keeps their mouth shut
p = piano, quietly in music
to have something down is to have it in writing

annotation.surface: A written effort to silence a reluctant witness.
annotation.walkthrough: The surface suggests censoring someone, which fits the answer's sense, but the wordplay is a simple run of three parts.
annotation.definitionFit: A clampdown is a concerted attempt to suppress something, such as crime or dissent.

entries.clue: Huge mistake whenever one enters court from the back (8)

indicators.note: the inner group goes inside the court abbreviation
reading CT from the back gives TC

blocks.note: CT (court) turned round
to err is to make a mistake
if = whenever, as in 'if it rains, I stay in'
I = one, the Roman numeral

annotation.surface: Every time someone walks into court they make an enormous blunder.
annotation.walkthrough: 'Huge mistake' reads as one phrase, but 'Huge' is the definition on its own. The mistake-whenever-one group is wrapped by the court abbreviation read from its end.
annotation.definitionFit: Terrific in its older sense means very great in size or intensity: a terrific noise.

entries.clue: Putting coat on, return work left in class (14)

indicators.note: 'in' means inside, so OP and L are placed within the word for class

blocks.note: to return an MP is to elect them
op = opus, a work
L = left
a rating is a class or grade

annotation.surface: Someone puts on a coat, goes back and does some work in a lesson.
annotation.walkthrough: 'Return' feels like 'go back', but here it is what voters do when they send a candidate to Parliament; the work and the left then go into the class.
annotation.definitionFit: Electroplating puts a thin coat of metal on an object by electrolysis.

entries.clue: Fanatic offered to support member of artistic establishment (5)

definitions.note: Fanatic is read as an adjective, as in 'fanatic supporters'.

indicators.note: in a down clue, the supporter sits underneath, so BID comes after RA

blocks.note: RA = Royal Academician, a member of the Royal Academy of Arts
to bid is to offer, at an auction

annotation.surface: A zealot puts up money to back an artist.
annotation.walkthrough: 'Artistic establishment' is the Royal Academy of Arts in London, whose members put RA after their names.
annotation.definitionFit: Rabid and fanatic both describe someone extreme and unreasoning in their views.

entries.clue: Miles shred old jumble (7)

blocks.note: miles away = far
a rag is a shred of cloth
O = old

annotation.surface: A man called Miles tears up an old muddle.
annotation.walkthrough: 'Miles' looks like a man's name doing something to paper, but it gives FAR.
annotation.definitionFit: A farrago is a confused mixture, a hotchpotch or jumble.

entries.clue: Memorable speed of light yacht at sea (6)

indicators.note: at sea means confused, so the letters of YACHT are jumbled

blocks.note: c is the physics symbol for the speed of light
YACHT rearranged

annotation.surface: A light, fast yacht on the water makes an unforgettable sight.
annotation.walkthrough: 'At sea' fits the yacht perfectly in the surface, which hides its job as an anagram signal.
annotation.definitionFit: A catchy tune is one that sticks in the memory.

entries.clue: Change of part, hence end of troublesome limp? (3,11)

definitions.text: Change of part, hence end of troublesome limp?

indicators.note: a change of the letters means rearranging them
the end of a word is its last letter

blocks.note: anagram fodder
last letter of troublesome
anagram fodder

annotation.surface: Swapping a worn body part ends a painful limp.
annotation.walkthrough: The whole clue is both the recipe and the description: rearrange PART HENCE, E and LIMP, and you get the operation that replaces a part and ends a limp.
annotation.definitionFit: A hip replacement swaps a damaged joint for an artificial one, often curing a limp.

entries.clue: Shortened dress soldier keeps shortening (9)

indicators.note: cut short, so GARB loses its last letter
to keep something is to hold it, so the soldier holds the shortened dress inside him

blocks.note: a marine is a soldier serving at sea
GARB (dress) without its last letter

annotation.surface: A soldier hangs on to a cut-down uniform while the tailor is still taking it up.
annotation.walkthrough: 'Shortening' looks like more trimming, but it is the cooking fat. Americans call fat for pastry shortening.
annotation.definitionFit: Shortening is fat used in baking to make pastry crumbly; margarine is one such fat.

entries.clue: Back massage ends in slight pop (5)

indicators.note: back means turned round, so RUB reads BUR
the two ends of slight are its first and last letters

blocks.note: a rub is a massage
first and last letters of slight

annotation.surface: A back massage finishes with a small crack of the spine.
annotation.walkthrough: 'Back massage' reads as one thing in the surface; 'Back' is the instruction to reverse RUB.
annotation.definitionFit: A plain synonym: a balloon that pops has burst.

entries.clue: Fancy a cry? (7)

blocks.note: a fancy is a whim
a = per, as in 'ten pounds a head'

annotation.surface: An invitation to have a good weep.
annotation.walkthrough: The surface reads as 'Would you like a cry?', with 'Fancy' as a verb; in the wordplay it is the noun WHIM.
annotation.definitionFit: A definition by example: a whimper is one particular kind of cry, low and broken.

entries.clue: Far too much poetry in that novel (2,5)

indicators.note: ODE goes inside the rearranged letters
novel means new, so the letters of THAT are made into something new

blocks.note: THAT rearranged
an ode is a poem

annotation.surface: A reader complains that a book has too many poems in it.
annotation.walkthrough: 'Novel' is the book in the surface and the anagram signal in the wordplay.
annotation.definitionFit: An idiom: doing something to death means overdoing it, far too much.

entries.clue: Gang violence postponing love for very eager Romeo (5)

indicators.note: to postpone is to put later, so the O moves to the end

blocks.note: agog = very eager
Romeo is R in the NATO alphabet
love = O, a nil score in tennis; it moves from inside AGOG to the end

annotation.surface: Street fighting breaks out as a lovestruck Romeo puts off his romance.
annotation.walkthrough: Build AGOG plus R, then postpone the O: it leaves its place in AGOG and goes last. Aggro is British slang for aggressive trouble-making.
annotation.definitionFit: Aggro is British slang for aggressive, violent behaviour, typically by gangs or football crowds.

entries.clue: Don’t stop stars performing? (6,2)

blocks.note: the Plough is a group of stars, also called the Big Dipper
on stage = performing

annotation.surface: A plea for celebrities to keep performing.
annotation.walkthrough: 'Stars' suggests performers, which chimes with 'performing', but it is the star pattern called the Plough.
annotation.definitionFit: To plough on is to keep going despite difficulty: not to stop.

entries.clue: Damage you’d expect to be contained by fireplace (5,4)

blocks.note: to go in something is to be contained by it
a grate is the metal frame of a fireplace

annotation.surface: Someone warns that harm is bound to be done to the hearth.
annotation.walkthrough: 'Damage' is the slangy 'What's the damage?', meaning the cost. 'Contained by' looks like a container signal, but here the phrase itself is the wordplay, meaning to enter.
annotation.definitionFit: The going rate is the usual price, the cost you would expect to pay.

entries.clue: Advanced child turned handle all at once (2,3,3)

indicators.note: turned round, so NAME reads EMAN

blocks.note: A = advanced, as in A level
a son is a child
a handle is a name; turned round it reads EMAN

annotation.surface: A precocious child spins a handle all in one go.
annotation.walkthrough: 'Handle' is slang for a name, not something you turn.
annotation.definitionFit: As one man means everyone together, simultaneously: all at once.

entries.clue: Council property unlikely to house private hospital (4,4)

indicators.note: TALL gives a home to OWN and H

blocks.note: a tall story is an unlikely one
your own room is a private one
H = hospital, on road signs

annotation.surface: A council building is an improbable site for a private clinic.
annotation.walkthrough: In the surface 'unlikely to house' is a prediction; in the wordplay 'unlikely' is TALL and 'to house' is the container signal.
annotation.definitionFit: A town hall is the building owned and used by a local council.

entries.clue: Bunting seen in town a lot, royalists put up (7)

indicators.note: the answer can be seen inside the following words
in a down clue, putting letters up reads them from bottom to top, i.e. backwards

blocks.note: the letters run across the end of town, all of 'a lot' and the start of royalists

annotation.surface: Flags are hung all over town as supporters of the monarchy put them up.
annotation.walkthrough: 'Bunting' is the flags in the surface but a bird in the answer: the ortolan is a small European bunting.
annotation.definitionFit: The ortolan is a small Eurasian songbird of the bunting family.

entries.clue: Anvil is iron on the outside, and every other part of course (5)

indicators.note: only the outside letters of iron are used
taking every other letter of course

blocks.note: first and last letters of iron
CoUrSe: letters 1, 3 and 5

annotation.surface: A blacksmith's anvil is iron on its surface, and all through.
annotation.walkthrough: The surface looks like a description of a blacksmith's tool; the answer is the tiny anvil-shaped bone in the middle ear.
annotation.definitionFit: The incus, Latin for anvil, is the middle-ear bone named for its shape.

entries.clue: Tom perhaps arrived hot, running from cold? (7)

definitions.note: The definition is a descriptive phrase for the noun rather than a synonym.

blocks.note: a tom is a male cat
arr. = arrived, on timetables
H = hot, on taps

annotation.surface: A tomcat turned up overheated, fleeing the chill.
annotation.walkthrough: 'Running from cold' seems to be escaping the weather; it is a runny nose caused by a cold, hence the question mark.
annotation.definitionFit: Catarrh is the build-up of mucus, the running nose that comes with a cold.

entries.clue: Go in search of fun and receive something that does the trick (6)

blocks.note: to gad about is to go out looking for fun
to get is to receive

annotation.surface: Advice to go out, enjoy yourself and come home with a useful tool.
annotation.walkthrough: The surface reads as one outing, but the clue splits at 'and': the first phrase is the old verb gad, as in gadding about.
annotation.definitionFit: A gadget is a small device that performs a particular job.

entries.clue: One should adopt a diplomatic attitude towards facial hair (7)

definitions.text: One should adopt a diplomatic attitude

blocks.note: to aim at is to aim towards
tache is British slang for a moustache

annotation.surface: Advice to be tactful about someone's moustache.
annotation.walkthrough: The surface is about tact over a moustache. The definition is the whole first part: an attaché works at an embassy, so should behave diplomatically.
annotation.definitionFit: An attaché is a member of an embassy's staff, whose job requires diplomacy.

entries.clue: Order military chief accepts is ridiculous (5)

indicators.note: to accept is to take in, so the chief's letters take the order inside them

blocks.note: CIC = commander-in-chief
OM = Order of Merit, a British honour

annotation.surface: A general's decision to receive a medal is called absurd.
annotation.walkthrough: 'Order' looks like a command given by the chief; here it is an honour, the Order of Merit.
annotation.definitionFit: A plain synonym: something comic is laughable, and so ridiculous.

entries.clue: Giant sounded tense (7)

indicators.note: sounded means spoken, so the answer sounds like the word for giant

blocks.note: a titan is a giant from Greek myth; the indicator says to use its sound, not its spelling

annotation.surface: A giant's voice comes out strained and nervous.
annotation.walkthrough: 'Tense' looks like an adjective describing the giant; here it is the verb, to tense a muscle.
annotation.definitionFit: A plain synonym in the verb sense, as when you brace a muscle before lifting.

entries.clue: Animated Lego, minute figure brought to life (5)

indicators.note: animated means full of movement, so the letters of LEGO move about

blocks.note: LEGO rearranged
m = minute

annotation.surface: A stop-motion film of a tiny Lego figure brings it to life.
annotation.walkthrough: 'Animated' fits Lego films perfectly, hiding the anagram signal. In Jewish folklore a golem is a clay figure brought to life.
annotation.definitionFit: A golem is a figure of clay magically brought to life in Jewish legend.

entries.clue: Pocketing a grand, trained men earn ninefold figure (9)

indicators.note: the rearranged letters put AG in their pocket
trained means shaped or taught, so the letters of MEN EARN are reshaped

blocks.note: MEN EARN rearranged
A + G, where G = grand, a thousand pounds

annotation.surface: Well-drilled workers take home a thousand pounds and earn nine times over.
annotation.walkthrough: The surface is all about money, and 'figure' looks like a sum; the answer is a nine-pointed diagram.
annotation.definitionFit: An enneagram is a nine-pointed figure, from Greek ennea, nine.

entries.clue: Resolve so many letters for Birmingham and Manchester? (8)

blocks.note: Birmingham and Manchester each have ten letters
a = for each, as in 'a pound a head'
both are English cities; the question mark marks them as examples

annotation.surface: A question about how many letters the names of two big cities take.
annotation.walkthrough: Count the letters: BIRMINGHAM and MANCHESTER both have ten, so the clue is saying 'ten a city'.
annotation.definitionFit: Tenacity is determination, firmness of purpose: resolve.

entries.clue: Fowl transfixed by male’s tail that’s lovely? (6)

definitions.text: Fowl transfixed by male’s tail that’s lovely?

blocks.note: the surface suggests a bird skewered, as on a spit; the meant sense is a bird spellbound
the male is the peacock, whose fanned tail is the famous lovely display; the bird watching it is his mate

annotation.surface: A bird stands spellbound by a male's gorgeous tail.
annotation.walkthrough: The peacock spreads its tail to court the female; the clue pictures her gazing at it, so the fowl is the peahen.
annotation.definitionFit: The peahen is the female peafowl, the audience for the peacock's display.
